title: Sunil Arora S/O Sh. Subhash Arora vs . on 24 July, 2020
full_text: Sunil Arora S/O Sh. Subhash Arora vs . on 24 July, 2020 IN THE COURT OF SH. RINKU JAIN METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE NI Act-02, WEST DISTRICT, TIS HAZARI COURTS, DELHI CC No.: 23243-16 U/s 138 NI Act In the matter of: Sunil Arora S/o Sh. Subhash Arora R/o I-144, 1st Floor, Kirti Nagar, New Delhi-110015 ...Complainant Vs. 1. M/S Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. through its director/s 2. Rakesh Bhalla (Managing Director) 3. Anita Bhalla (Authorized Signatory) 4. Ramesh Chand Bhalla (Director) All at F-191 E, Street No. 2, Laxmi Nagar, New Delhi-110092 ..... Accused DATE OF INSTITUTION : 08.10.2016 DATE WHEN JUDGMENT RESERVED : 24.02.2020 DATE OF JUDGMENT : 24.07.2020 DECISION : Accused No. 1 & 3 Convicted, Accused No. 2 declared proclaimed person vide order dated 24.01.2019. Accused No. 4 Acquitted. CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 1 of 13 BRIEF STATEMENT OF FACTS FOR THE DECISION:- 1. Shorn off unnecessary details, the case of the complainant as narrated in the complaint is that the accused company is into business of planning & fixing group trips and booking of hotels, tickets etc and other accused are its directors. Complainant had friendly relations with the accused persons as their office was situated in premises owned by one of the relatives of the complainant. In the month of August 2015, on the suggestion of accused persons, complainant collected Rs. 7,50,000/- for advance booking of air tickets for total eight members i.e. family of complainant and his friend to travel to U.S.A. via Dubai and U.K. in the months from April 2016 to June 2016. Complainant paid the said sum of Rs. 7,50,000/- to the accused persons in September 2015 for which accused booked eight tickets and assured the complainant that there shall be no problem in getting the Visas in group. Accused failed to provide the booked tickets to the complainant till June 2016 after which accused in discharge of its legal liability issued cheque bearing no. 000049 dated 22.06.2016 for a sum of Rs. 7,50,000/- drawn on HDFC Bank Vikas Marg, Delhi Ex.CW1/1 (hereinafter referred to as 'cheque in question'). Upon presentation the cheque in question was returned dishonored twice, last vide cheque return memo dated 03.08.2016 for the reasons "Present with document" Ex.CW1/2. Accused were informed about the dishonour of cheque in question but accused avoided the complainant. This constrained the complainant to send a legal demand notice dated 22.08.2016 Ex.CW1/4. No heed was paid by the accused to the said notice, resultantly, the present complaint was filed. 2. Pre-summoning evidence was led, cognizance of the offence u/s 138 NI Act was taken against the accused and summons were issued against all the CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 2 of 13 accused. Thereafter, accused company entered appearance through Accused no. 3 and 4. Accused no. 2 never appeared in court and was declared a proclaimed person later. Copy of complaint as well as of documents were supplied to the accused. Subsequent to that notice u/s. 251 CrPC for offence u/s. 138 N.I. Act was served upon the accused company on 13.07.2018 through accused no. 3 & 4 in which accused did not plead guilty and claimed trial. In the plea of defence, signatures on cheques in question were admitted to be of accused no. 3. The defence of the accused was that accused no. 3 & 4 did not know the complainant or how the cheque in question came into possession of the complainant. Affairs of accused company were looked after by accused no.2 and not by accused no 3 & 4. They denied the receipt of legal demand notice and liability qua the cheque in question. Evidence of the complainant 3. Complainant examined himself as CW1 and Akhilesh Jha, Banker of accused as CW2. CW1 reiterated the facts of his complaint in his evidence affidavit. He relied upon documents Ex.CW1/1 to Ex.CW1/5. He was duly cross-examined by the Ld. Counsel for accused. 4. In his cross-examination, complainant deposed that he came to know about the accused company from one Rajeev Malhotra, who introduced him to Rakesh Bhalla (accused no.2). Rakesh Bhalla told him about packages for different destinations. He denied that Rajeev Malhotra was actively involved in the present transaction. He named the eight persons for whom the tickets were booked through the accused and admitted that all of them were his family members contrary to his complaint in which he claimed that tickets were booked for his family and his friend's family. He made payment to CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 3 of 13 accused no. 2 & 3. He could not tell whether Rajeev Malhotra was also a director of the accused company or he was involved in day to day affairs of accused company. He could not bring any record regarding payment of Rs. 7.5 lacs to the accused. Cheque in question was given to him by accused no.2. 5. CW2 Sh. Akhilesh Jha, Assistant Manager, HDFC Bank, Vikas Marg brought certified copy of statement of bank account of accused Ex. CW2/A reflecting dishonor of cheque in question twice i.e. on 24.06.2016 & 03.08.2016. He brought cover letter Ex. CW1/B which mentioned reason for dishonor of cheque in question on 24.06.2016 as "insufficient funds". Defence of the accused 6. Thereafter, statement of accused no. 3 & 4 was u/s 313 CrPC in which all the incriminating material was put to them and they denied all the allegations levelled against them. They have taken the same defence as was taken by them at time of framing of notice u/s 251 Cr. P.C. In case of accused No.1/company, which is a juristic person, no separate statement under section 313 Cr. .P.C. was recorded as accused no. 1 has been duly represented through accused no. 3 & 4 since beginning of the trial. No separate or specific defence was taken by accused no. 3 & 4 with respect to accused company and at the same time, no objection was raised by them at the time of final arguments regarding the fact that no separate statement u/s 313 of CrPC was ever recorded qua the accused company. Both accused No. 3 and 4 have taken the defence that they have no concern with the complainant and that they had no role to play in the day to day affairs of the company/ accused No. 1. At the same, accused no. 4 had submitted in his respective statement that prior to the day/ date of the issuance of the cheque in question, he had resigned from the CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 4 of 13 directorship of the accused company No.1. Accused no. 3 & 4s have not led any evidence on behalf of accused company or their own behalf. 7. The factual position being thus, the legal bench mark which is to be satisfied in order to constitute an offence u/s 138 N. I. Act: (a) That the accused issued cheque in favour of the payee/complainant on an account maintained by him to discharge legal liability in whole or in part. (b) That the cheque was presented within stipulated time by the complainant for encashment. (c) That the cheque was dishonoured on presentation because of the amount of money standing to the credit of the account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with the bank. (d) That the demand for the payment of the said amount of money is made by giving a legal demand notice within 30 days from the receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid. (e) That the accused fails to make payment of the cheque amount to complainant within 15 days, after receiving of the legal demand notice. 8. Being cumulative, a person who had drawn the cheque is deemed to have committed an offence u/s 138 N. I. Act when all the aforementioned ingredients are satisfied. 9. That Ld. Counsel for complainant argued the matter at length. Ld. defence counsel also argued the matter in rebuttal. I have heard the submissions of both parties and gone through the judicial file. CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 5 of 13 10. On analysis of the facts and legal positions stated above, the court finds the parties to be at variance on two of the primary issues i.e. whether the legal demand notice was served upon the accused and whether the cheque in question was issued in favour of the complainant in order to discharge the legal liability of the accused to repay the complainant for the payment received for booking of air tickets for eight persons. Service of legal demand notice 11. The first defence of the accused is non service of legal notice. It is contended on behalf of the accused that the accused did not receive the legal demand notice & the same was deliberately sent by complainant on wrong address and therefore the ingredients of the offence under Section 138 NI Act are not fulfilled and this would inexorably result in the acquittal of accused. However, this claim of the accused for acquittal is not sustainable in the eyes of law. 12. In view of the authoritative Judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhadmmed and Ors. (2007) 6 SCC 555, the rigour of the requirement of service of legal notice has been reduced to an almost vanishing point in Section 138 NI Act jurisprudence. The Hon'ble Supreme Court while discussing the true intent behind the service of legal demand notice as a precursor to the launch of prosecution has quite categorically held that the service of summons of the court is opportunity enough for the accused to pay the cheque amount and evade prosecution, any accused who fails to pay the amount within 15 days of the service of summons, clearly cannot shield himself behind the technical demand of non service of legal notice. The relevant extract of the decision deserves to be CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 6 of 13 quoted in extenso:- ''17. It is also to be borne in mind that the requirement of giving of notice is a clear departure from the rule of criminal law, where there is no stipulation of giving of a notice before filing a complaint. Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice sent by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of the complaint under Section 138 of Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submits to the court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with the summons) and, therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the court along with the copy of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of the G.C.Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act. In our view, any other interpretation of the proviso, would defeat the very object of the legislation''. 13. Admittedly, the accused has failed to pay the cheque amount within a period of 15 days from the date of service of summons of her appearance before this court. Therefore, in view of the above stated Judgment passed by Hon'ble Apex Court, the fact of non service of legal demand notice will not come to aid the accused and therefore, the accused cannot claim acquittal on this ground. 14. The non service of legal notice challenge having been met, let us now turn to the core issue in this case and examine "whether the cheque in question can be said to have been issued in discharge of legal liability or not''. CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 7 of 13 Existence of legally enforceable debt or liability 15. It has been admitted by the accused no. 1 through accused no. 3 & 4 that the cheque in question was drawn upon the bank account maintained in the name of accused no. 1 and accused no. 3 having signed the same. Once these foundational facts are admitted and a factual base is established, presumption of cheque having been issued in discharge of legally recoverable debt and drawn for lawful consideration arises by virtue of Section 118 (a) and Section 139 of N. I. Act. 16. According to the scheme of N. I. Act , on proof of foundational facts, a presumption arises as to the cheques having been issued in discharge of the legal liability and the burden is on the accused to rebut the said presumption. This clearly is an instance of the rule of "reverse onus" in action where it is incumbent on the accused to lead what can be called as "negative evidence". The evidence of a character, not to prove a fact affirmative, but to lead evidence to show non-existence of a liability. Keeping in view, this is a departure from the cardinal rule of "presumption of innocence" in favour of the accused, keeping in mind that the negative evidence is not easy to be led by its very nature. It is now clearly settled that the accused can reverse this presumption on a scale of preponderance of probabilities. Lack of legally enforceable debt in favour of the complainant need not be proved to the hilt beyond all reasonable doubts. Preponderance is superiority in weight. Preponderance of probabilities means more probable than not and superior in evidentiary weight than the opposite. 17. In Rangappa Vs Sri Mohan (2010)11 SCC 441, it was observed that CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 8 of 13 Section 139 of N.I. Act is stated to be an example of a reverse onus clause which is in tune with the legislator intend of improving the credibility of negotiable instruments. Section 138 of N. I. Act provides for speedy remedy in a criminal forum, in relation to dishonour of cheques. 18. In case of Kumar Exports vs. Sharma Carpets ,(2009) 2 SCC 513, the Hon'ble Supreme Court had held:- The accused under Section 138 NI Act has two options. He can either show that the consideration and debt did not exit or that under the particular circumstances of the case, the non existence of consideration and debt is so probable that a prudent man ought to suppose that no consideration and debt existed. To rebut the statutory presumption, an accused is not expected to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt as it is expected of the complainant in a criminal trial. The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, the court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the non existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time, it is clear that bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of debt, apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Something which his probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or there non existence was so CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 9 of 13 probably that a prudent man under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist. Apart from adducing direct evidence to prove that the note in question, was not supported by consideration or that he had not incurred any debt or liability, the accused may also rely upon the circumstantial evidence and if the circumstances so relied upon are so compelling, the burden may likewise shift again on the complainant. The accused may also rely upon presumptions of fact, for instance, those mentioned in Section 114 of the Evidence Act to rebut the presumptions arises under Section 118 and 139 of NI Act''. 19. As discussed above, it is clear that the accused need not discharge his liability beyond the shadow of reasonable doubts. He just needs to create holes in the case set out by the complainant. Accused can either say that the version brought forth by the complainant is inherently unbelievable and, therefore, the prosecution cannot stand or the accused can give his version of the story and say that on the basis of his version the story of the complainant cannot be believed. In the first situation, the accused has nothing to do but to point inherit inconsistencies in the case of the complainant. 20. So far as the facts of liability is concerned, in view of mandatory presumption of law as discussed above, if any accepted signed cheque has been produced by the complainant, there cannot be any inherent lacuna in the existence of the liability. But then definitely, accused can point loop holes in the story of the complainant by impeaching the credit of the witness during his cross-examination. The accused can discharge his burden by demonstrating the preponderance of probabilities coming in its way. CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 10 of 13 21. In the case in hand, defence of accused no. 3 & 4 is that they don't have any knowledge of the present transaction and they were not involved in day to day affairs of the accused company. Complainant in his cross-examination specifically stated that payment was made to accused no. 2 & 3. Cheque in question bears the signatures of accused no. 3 which have been admitted by her. Once the signatures are admitted the onus was on accused no. 3 to rebut the presumption that she was not actively involved in day to day affairs of the accused no. 1/company. Not even an iota of evidence has been led by accused no. 3 to prove and corroborate her assertion that she had no knowledge about the present transaction or that she was not involved in day to day affairs of the accused company. Therefore, in the opinion of this court the assertions of accused no. 3 are bald and are not sustainable at the mere ipse dixit of the accused no. 3. 22. As far as accused No. 4 is concerned the argument of ld counsel for accused that he was not involved in day to day affairs of the accused company is worthy of acceptance as in the legal demand notice, complaint and the evidence affidavit of the complainant no specific role has been attributed to accused No. 4. It is evident that no averments were made against accused no. 4 except stating "accused persons" in general throughout the complaint and evidence affidavit as well. Complainant cannot by merely alleging that every action of accused no. 1 was done through all the accused persons, array accused no. 4 for the offence u/s 138 read with section 141 NI Act. Complainant had to specify exact role of accused no. 4. Complainant has miserably failed to prove the role of accused no. 4. It is trite law that for an accused, who is a director, to be held vicariously liable u/s 141 of N.I Act, ought to be in charge of, and responsible to the company for CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 11 of 13 the conduct of the business of the company. Accused no. 4 not being in such a position, inevitably lead to a conclusion that he cannot be held vicariously liable under the provision of section 141 of NI Act. 23. Ld. counsel for accused argued that all the accused are liable to be acquitted as complainant lacked financial capacity to advance a sum of Rs. 7,50,000/- as alleged in the complainant. Apart from a question regarding the production of record of payment of Rs. 7,50,000/- in the cross-examination of the complainant, throughout the trial, defence of accused was ignorance of the fact of present transaction even at the stage of recording of statement u/s 313 CrPC. The same does not appear to be sufficient to hold the accused innocent and this court is not in concurrence with argument of Ld. counsel for accused. 24. In view of the discussion above, Accused no.1/ company and accused no. 3 have failed to prove their defence and in rebutting the presumption of legal liability even on the scale of preponderance of probabilities and the defence of the accused no.1 & 3 cannot be termed as a plausible defence. The presumption of legal liability u/s 118 (a) r/w S-139 NI Act has gone un-rebutted qua accused no. 1 & 3 and the complainant has successfully proved the basic ingredients of the offence u/s 138 read with section 141 of NI Act. The present case also appears to be a fit case where benefit of doubt can be extended to accused no. 4. 25. Thus in view of aforementioned analysis of evidence, considerations and discussion accused no. 1 M/s Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. stands convicted for the offence u/s 138 NI Act. Accused no.3 Anita Bhalla being director of accused no.1/company & signatory of cheque in question is held vicariously liable and is also convicted for offence punishable u/s 138 r/w section CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 12 of 13 141 N.I. Act committed by accused no.1/company. At the same time, Accused no.4 Ramesh Chand Bhalla stands acquitted of the offence u/s 138 NI Act 1881. Announced on CISCO WEBEX on this day of 24.07.2020 (Rinku Jain) MM( NI Act )-02 (West)/ THC, Delhi CC No. 23243-16 Sunil Arora V. Shubh Manglam Travels Pvt. Ltd. Page 13 of 13
